Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For police violence, water/flooding and soil/outdoor smells are hard to reconcile as primary trauma-linked triggers when the rest of the profile contains no content suggesting a water, outdoor, or environmental trauma context. Bus riding could fit policing/public surveillance, but these other triggers point toward a different trauma setting.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells
issues.explanation: The appraisal of lost connection to community/culture is possible after police violence, but in this profile it is not supported by the selected triggers or memories, which center on acute sensory reliving and bodily threat rather than social exclusion, community rupture, or cultural shame. It feels disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, emotionless recall can coexist with reliving, but combining complete numb detachment with full multisensory reliving and bodily reenactment as parallel core memory experiences is somewhat tensioned. More importantly, the reliving items imply a very specific embodied trauma scene, yet the trigger set does not reflect cues plausibly tied to that scene.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: Mirror checking is difficult to explain from the rest of the profile. The threat items concern rapid bodily danger detection, reading faces, and sleep vigilance; the memories concern reliving; and the appraisals concern distrust/contamination/community loss. Mirror checking suggests appearance/body checking or checking for signs on oneself, but no associated appraisal or memory content supports it. It does not cohere well with the police violence formulation here.

vignette: Rashmi had always felt a sense of pride in her community and culture. As a counselor working with South Asian youth, she was committed to creating safe spaces for them to share their struggles and find support. But that all changed one fateful day when she was stopped by police on her way home from work. The memory of the event still feels like a visceral blow: the sound of the officer's voice, the feeling of his hands on her body, the smell of the earthy soil beneath her feet as she was forced to kneel. Since that day, Rashmi has found it increasingly difficult to ride public buses, which always seem to transport her back to that moment. The sensation of being confined and vulnerable is suffocating. When she catches a whiff of outdoor smells - like freshly cut grass or damp soil - she's instantly transported back to the scene. Even the sight of police officers on the street can send her heart racing, as if her body has learned to react before her mind even registers the threat. As a result, Rashmi has begun to avoid social contacts with friends and family who remind her of life before the incident. She's started to cover her face with her hands when she feels anxious or overwhelmed, as if hiding behind a physical barrier can shield her from the world. At home, she finds herself constantly checking mirrors, scanning for potential threats lurking just out of sight. But it's not just external triggers that pose a threat; Rashmi's own body has become a source of fear. She feels like she's always on high alert, ready to spring into action at the slightest hint of danger. Her mind is constantly racing, searching faces and body language for signs of deception or hostility. Even in her sleep, she's vigilant, lying awake as her brain struggles to relax. When memories of the event do surface, they're often accompanied by a strange sense of numbness. It's as if Rashmi is observing herself from outside her own body, recalling the details with detachment. But when the memories come flooding back in vivid detail - the sights, sounds, smells, and sensations all at once - it feels like she's reliving the trauma anew. Her body seems to reenact the experience, twisting into the same positions as if trying to relive the pain. Rashmi can't shake the feeling that the event has left her contaminated in some fundamental way. She feels like she's lost touch with her community and culture, like she no longer belongs. People seem untrustworthy now, their smiles and laughter hiding secrets and lies. Even her own reflection in the mirror seems distorted, as if she's gazing at a stranger. As a counselor, Rashmi is acutely aware of the irony - she's trained to help others process trauma, yet she can't seem to escape her own. The weight of these emotions has taken a toll on her relationships and work; she feels like she's living in a constant state of hypervigilance, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. It was only when a client finally asked Rashmi why she seemed so distant that she realized how far she'd retreated into herself. Something about the genuine concern in the client's eyes pierced through her defenses, and Rashmi felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, it was time to confront the trauma head-on, rather than trying to outrun it. With a deep breath, Rashmi made the decision to seek help - not as a counselor, but as a patient in need of healing herself.
